newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovaks launch drive to elect president directly.
newsitem.headline: Slovaks launch drive to elect president directly.

text.p: Slovakia's main opposition parties on Thursday launched a drive for direct presidential elections, a move condemned by Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar as against national interests.

Ivan Simko, vice-chairman of the Christian Democratic Movement (KDH) and head of a petition committee seeking a referendum on the issue, told about 1,500 people who braved bitter weather in Bratislava's main square, that the move was sought to reinforce the independent position of the president.
"We want to have a president who would enjoy a status fully independent on the political parties," Simko said.

The referendum is seen as an attempt to prevent any possibility that Meciar, whom the opposition regards as heavy handed and autocratic, would assume presidential powers before the election of a new president.
The current term of President Michal Kovac, elected in March 1993 by parliament, expires in March 1998, six months before Slovakia's next general election set for the following October.

"Such a referendum is not in the interest of Slovakia, it's merely in the interest of a single politician, Kovac, and the political opposition," Meciar told a monthly rally of supporters of his ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia.

In the present parliament, the ruling coalition and the opposition cannot agree on a common condidate for president and neither can garner the three-fifths majority necessary in the 150-seat house to push through their own choice.
"It is almost sure that the (two) political camps will not agree (on a president) and this could lead to a serious political crisis in the country," Simko said.

According to the constitution which came into effect after Czechoslovakia split in two in 1993, Meciar, an avowed political foe of Kovac, would assume presidential powers in the event of an indecisive vote.
Simko warned that the interim president could not, for example, sign new laws which could paralyse the legislature.
"There would also be nobody to accept the resignation of the government after the general election so we could be saddled with a virtually indismissible cabinet," he said.
If the 350,000 signature minimum needed were reached, Kovac would be empowered to call a referendum within 90 days. At least 50 percent of the electorate must vote in a referendum to make it valid.
A simple majority of those voting would be needed to pass a resolution that the president be elected directly by the people.
